shortest consent in the language; xíng ba = reluctant "fiiine." Also read háng = "row/line" — different meaning, mind the gloss you hear.

Glue — grammar

exclamations: tài…le, zhēn, hǎo

Template: Tài + Adj + le! / Zhēn + Adj / Hǎo + Adj

the reaction layer of chat — enthusiasm lives here, not in hěn

Zhè fēngjǐng hǎo měi a!
Nǐ zhēn shì tài kù le!

Foreigner traps

  • tài REQUIRES its le: tài hǎo without le is a song lyric, not a sentence.
  • zhēn doesn't take the le: zhēn hǎo ✓, zhēn hǎo le ✗ — tài owns the frame tài + Adj + le.
  • hǎo + Adj is instant-reaction (hǎo lèi a); hěn + Adj is a weather report — pick by temperature, not grammar.
  • Stacking is native: Tài hǎochī le, zhēn bàng! — enthusiasm compounds instead of picking one form.

yǒudiǎn vs yìdiǎn

Template: yǒudiǎn + Adj ("a bit too…") vs Adj + yìdiǎn ("a bit more…")

softening complaints vs requesting a change

Jīntiān yǒudiǎn lěng, duō chuān yí jiàn.
Wǒ yǒudiǎn è le, wǒmen chī diǎn dōngxi ba.

Foreigner traps

  • Order decides the job: yǒudiǎn + Adj complains (yǒudiǎn guì); Adj + yìdiǎn requests change (piányi yìdiǎn).
  • yǒudiǎn leans negative — mild praise is hái búcuò, never yǒudiǎn hǎochī (which snarks 'only somewhat tasty').
  • yǒudiǎn is written as one word and spoken fast — a slow, deliberate yǒu…diǎn turns 'a bit' into 'quite a lot', the opposite of softening.

Native notes — the reaction economy, soft complaints, and pointing like a local

Reacting is a social duty

tài…le, zhēn, and hǎo are the currency of chat. Good news answered with a flat hǎo reads as cold or jealous — natives layer it: Tài hǎo le! Zhēn bàng! and add wā or a sticker in texting. hěn is for weather reports; enthusiasm lives in today's glue.

yǒudiǎn is the complaint softener

yǒudiǎn guì, yǒudiǎn là pre-frames criticism as minor so it doesn't attack the cook or the host — it's politeness physics. Praise doesn't take yǒudiǎn: mild approval is hái búcuò or tǐng hǎo. And remember the order rule: yǒudiǎn + Adj complains, Adj + yìdiǎn requests.

Chongqing pointing: the diǎn set

lēdiǎn (here) is the first of a three-piece local set — nèdiǎn (there) lands day 14, nǎdiǎn (where) day 18; the standard twins are zhèlǐ / nàlǐ / nǎlǐ. Use lēdiǎn with the taxi driver or the shop auntie and you'll see the price change. The field guide drills the accent; the sprint drills the reflex.

hǎo + Adj is the quiet intensifier

hǎo lèi a, hǎo kuài a — casual speech loves hǎo as 'so' without the exclamation-mark energy of tài. Texting uses it constantly (hǎo xiǎng nǐ — miss you so much). Learn it as a dial: hěn states, hǎo feels, tài shouts.
